we followed a boy named Sruli as he filled his year with extravagant escapades and unthinkable pursuits.

Two years ago was no different. After davening and the Yom Tov meal, my father and I set out for Dave’s house with our shofar in hand.

He lives two long miles from our Chabad House. It was a scorching hot day, and we arrived tired, sweaty, and eager to help a fellow Yid. We knocked on the door, but nobody answered, so we walked around to the back of the house. There we saw Dave’s wife and daughter relaxing.

“We’re so sorry that you can’t blow the shofar for Dave this year,” they said. “He’s out surfing.”

“No problem,” Tatty said. “I’ll blow it for just the two of you. But if you don’t mind, let’s walk towards the beach so we can get as close to Dave as possible.”

When we got near the water, we could see Dave out in the distance, riding the waves with some friends. Tatty turned to Dave’s wife and said, “I’m going to try blowing the shofar so loud that Dave can hear it all the way out in the ocean!”

Tatty took a deep breath, and blew the shofar with all of his might. Again and again he blew, until all of the tekios were finished.

He turned to Dave’s wife and cheerfully concluded, “I hope that when Dave comes home later, he’ll say, ‘Y’know, I think I heard the shofar while I was surfing!’ And you can say, ‘You sure did!’”

We all laughed, and then wished Dave’s wife and daughter a “Shana Tova!” as we headed back to the Chabad House for Tashlich.

Months passed, and we forgot all about the shofar blowing on the beach. Summer time came, and soon it was Tisha B’Av.

Like I said before, Dave always comes to shul on Tisha B’Av. Why then? Well, there are many Yidden who go to shul only once each year—on Yom Kippur. Dave promised his mother that he wouldn’t be a “once-a-year Jew” like all the rest; he would at least be a “twice-a-year Jew”. So he searched the calendar for a second time to show up to shul, and decided that Tisha B’Av was the day. (Why he didn’t choose a happier time like Simchas Torah, Purim, or Shavuos, I have no idea, but he didn’t ask me…)

That Tisha B’Av afternoon, however, Dave had brought someone else along with him—a teenage boy with a tefillin bag in hand. The boy put down the bag, reached for a Siddur, and started putting on his tefillin.

A local Yid who owns tefillin? Tatty curiously walked over to their table. “Dave! I’m happy you’re here! And who is this young man?”

The boy told Tatty his name, and then added proudly, “I put tefillin on every day, and it’s all because of you, rabbi!”

Quite surprised, Tatty asked him to explain. This is what the teenager said:

“Ten months ago, my father, twin brother, and I went out

surfing with Dave. We were having a great time on the waves, when I suddenly heard a noise that sounded like a shofar’s blast. ‘Impossible!’ I thought to myself, ‘There’s no way I’m hearing a shofar out here in the ocean!’ But then I heard it again, and again. By now, there was no mistaking the noise—it was definitely a shofar. And as I learned later that day, it was your shofar; the one you blew for us as we surfed those ocean waves.

“Hearing that heavenly sound shook me to my core. Right then and there, I decided that I want to go to Israel to study Judaism. As soon as we returned to shore, I told my father how I felt, and we began looking into options. Before I knew it, I was on my way to the Holy Land!

I enrolled in a beginners' yeshiva, and spent the next few months soaking in everything I could about my new heritage. Hands down, those were the best months of my life. Back at home, I now put on tefillin every day!”

Tatty was amazed that someone who was completely not observant just a few short months ago, would begin to wear tefillin on his own. He invited the boy to spend a Shabbos in our home. One Shabbos led to another, and he became fully shomer Shabbos.

Today, that boy’s twin brother and father are steady visitors at Chabad, and each have their own pair of tefillin. The teenager himself lives in Eretz Yisroel, and is completely frum —all because of the power of shofar.

We are inspired by their newfound commitment to Yiddishkeit, and even more inspired to strengthen our commitment to mivtzoyim. We can’t wait to get back out there, and blow shofar for every Yid!
